title: Breaking boundaries to creatively generate value: The role of resourcefulness in entrepreneurship
paper_role: theory foundation
context: general entrepreneurship; entrepreneurial resourcefulness; value creation under resource constraints
main_topic: entrepreneurial resourcefulness
research_question_or_purpose: To explain the role of resourcefulness in entrepreneurship and outline how entrepreneurs creatively generate value under constraints.
abstract: Entrepreneurial resourcefulness is a concept that resonates with practitioners and scholars alike from a diverse set of theoretical and empirical backgrounds. Despite the prevalence and promise of this concept, the literature on entrepreneurial resourcefulness is fragmented and lacks cohesion in how it is labeled, conceptualized, measured, and deployed. In many cases, it appears that bringing resources to bear for entrepreneurial purposes is taken for granted, which limits theoretical development of if and how ventures emerge and grow. In this editorial, we explore the theoretical underpinnings of resourcefulness, offer a definition, and provide a roadmap for future scholarship. In addition, we introduce the six articles that comprise the Special Issue on entrepreneurial resourcefulness, discuss their contributions, and explore how they relate to our overall perspective on resources and resourcefulness. It is our hope that this Special Issue will mobilize additional scholarship to enhance our knowledge on resourcefulness, which we view as a fundamental part of entrepreneurship.

The literature on resourcefulness is fragmented and lacks conceptual cohesion.
The paper positions resourcefulness as relevant for understanding how ventures emerge and grow.

best_use_in_thesis: Use as a theory-foundation paper to support the idea that entrepreneurs, including possible digital freelancers, create value by mobilizing limited resources under constraints.

title: Reputation and new venture performance in online markets: The moderating role of market crowding
paper_role: empirical fit paper
context: platform-mediated online markets; new ventures; reputation; market crowding; online marketplace performance
main_topic: reputation, new venture performance, and market crowding in online markets
research_question_or_purpose: To examine how reputation affects new venture performance in online markets and whether market crowding moderates the reputation-performance relationship.
abstract: Reputation represents an important driver of new venture performance. This article shows that the performance benefits of reputation are substantially contingent on ventures' market conditions. My study of 797,087 sales transactions by 5760 new ventures in 119 platform-mediated online markets provides strong evidence that market crowding attenuates the reputation-performance relationship. Ventures benefit 38% to 42% more from a favorable reputation when they compete in an uncrowded versus crowded market. By disentangling the underlying mechanisms of reputation, the study allows for more accurate predictions about why, when, and how ventures benefit from reputation.
introduction: The introduction frames new ventures as facing essential challenges in establishing performance and credibility, especially in online markets where low entry barriers increase competition and make markets crowded and noisy. The paper argues that reputation is important because it helps ventures overcome uncertainty by signaling quality and creating competitive advantage. However, the introduction also problematizes the assumption that reputation benefits ventures equally across all market conditions. In platform-mediated online markets, crowding can reduce the value of reputation because many competing offerings make it harder for any single venture to stand out. The study therefore positions market crowding as a key contingency that may weaken the positive relationship between reputation and new venture performance. This framing leads to the empirical question of whether reputation improves performance less strongly in crowded markets than in uncrowded markets.

Online markets often have low entry barriers, which can increase market crowding.
Reputation is framed as both a quality signal and a source of competitive advantage.

sample_or_data: 797,087 sales transactions by 5,760 new ventures in 119 platform-mediated online markets
key_findings: Reputation improves new venture performance in online markets, but the performance benefit of reputation is weaker in crowded markets. The study finds that ventures gain more from favorable reputation when they compete in less crowded markets.

title: Actions in words: How entrepreneurs use diversified and changing speech acts to achieve funding success
paper_role: empirical fit paper
context: crowdfunding; entrepreneurial narratives; resource acquisition; linguistic cues; funding campaign descriptions
main_topic: entrepreneurial speech acts, narrative variation, and crowdfunding success
research_question_or_purpose: To examine how the diversity of speech acts and changes among speech acts in entrepreneurial crowdfunding narratives influence funding success.
abstract: This study examines how linguistic attributes in entrepreneurs' funding campaign descriptions influence crowdfunding outcomes. Instead of studying individual linguistic attributes separately, the paper treats an entrepreneurial narrative as a portfolio of speech acts. Speech acts are actions performed through words, such as asserting facts, expressing feelings, making commitments, or directing listeners toward behavior. Drawing on speech act theory and the stimuli variation perspective, the study analyzes how speech act diversity and changes between speech acts affect funding success. Using 28,000 crowdfunding campaigns and a supervised machine-learning approach, the authors find that entrepreneurs who use more diverse speech acts and change more frequently among them are more likely to achieve funding success. The study also finds inverted U-shaped relationships between assertive, directive, and expressive speech acts and crowdfunding success.
introduction: The introduction positions entrepreneurial narratives as important tools for resource acquisition, especially in crowdfunding contexts where entrepreneurs and potential funders do not meet face to face. In this setting, language becomes a primary mechanism through which entrepreneurs present their venture, communicate credibility, persuade audiences, and attract financial resources. Prior research has examined individual linguistic attributes in entrepreneurial narratives, but this paper argues that narratives should also be understood as portfolios of linguistic actions. The study focuses on speech acts because entrepreneurs do not merely describe ventures with words; they perform actions through language, such as asserting facts, expressing emotion, committing to future action, or directing funders toward support. The paper therefore asks whether the diversity of speech acts and the frequency of changes between speech acts make narratives more persuasive and improve crowdfunding success.

key_findings: Entrepreneurs who use a greater diversity of speech acts and frequently change from one speech act to another in campaign narratives are more likely to achieve crowdfunding success. title: The frugal entrepreneur: A self-regulatory perspective of resourceful entrepreneurial behavior
paper_role: theory foundation / variable-definition paper
context: entrepreneurial resourcefulness; frugality; self-regulation; resource use behavior; entrepreneurship under constraints
main_topic: frugality, self-control, and resourceful entrepreneurial behavior
research_question_or_purpose: To develop and test a self-regulatory perspective of entrepreneurial resourcefulness by distinguishing trait frugality from self-control and examining how both predict different entrepreneurial resource-use behaviors.
abstract: This study complements existing resourcefulness research by arguing that resourceful entrepreneurial behaviors do not arise only from environmental constraints. Entrepreneurs may also self-impose constraints on resource acquisition and deployment. The paper introduces frugality as a distinct construct in entrepreneurship research and differentiates it from self-control. It proposes that frugality predicts resource-use behaviors based on long-held preferences, such as effectuation and bricolage, while self-control predicts behaviors based on known goals or end states, such as causation and pre-commitments. After developing and validating a new measure of entrepreneurial frugality, the study finds support for the proposed self-regulatory framework and outlines future research opportunities for studying frugality in entrepreneurial behavior.
introduction: The article begins from the premise that resourcefulness is widely seen as important for entrepreneurship, but that most prior research explains resourceful behavior as a response to external or environmental constraints. The authors argue that this view is incomplete because entrepreneurs may also act resourcefully due to internal, self-imposed constraints and personal preferences regarding resource acquisition and use. The introduction therefore shifts attention from only asking how entrepreneurs respond to scarcity toward asking why some entrepreneurs may prefer to conserve, stretch, or creatively deploy resources even when external constraints are not the sole driver. To develop this argument, the paper introduces trait frugality as a construct relevant to entrepreneurship and distinguishes it from self-control. Frugality is positioned as a stable preference for careful resource use, while self-control is connected to regulating behavior toward known goals or end states. This framing allows the authors to connect different self-regulatory orientations to different entrepreneurial behaviors, especially bricolage, effectuation, causation, and pre-commitment behaviors.

title: What's in a logo? The impact of complex visual cues in equity crowdfunding
paper_role: empirical fit paper / method paper
context: equity crowdfunding; visual cues; venture perception; information asymmetry; funding decisions
main_topic: logo complexity, visual cues, perceived innovativeness, and crowdfunding investment
research_question_or_purpose: To examine whether and how low-validity visual cues, specifically logo complexity, influence backers' perceptions of venture innovativeness and funding decisions in equity crowdfunding.
abstract: Visual cues are common on crowdfunding platforms, but their effect on backer behavior is not fully understood. This study develops a disfluency-based heuristic framework to explain how low-validity visual cues can shape perceptions of early-stage ventures. Drawing on processing fluency theory and visual heuristics, the article argues that backers automatically process visual cues and that the perceived ease or difficulty of processing these cues becomes a heuristic for evaluating ventures. The study focuses on logo complexity, arguing that more complex logos may feel less familiar, more unique, more original, and more novel, causing backers to perceive ventures as more innovative. Because innovativeness is valued by backers, logo complexity can positively affect funding decisions. The authors test this argument using three studies: a survey, a field study, and an experiment.
introduction: The introduction frames equity crowdfunding as a setting characterized by information asymmetry, where backers must evaluate early-stage ventures with incomplete information. Prior crowdfunding research has largely focused on high-validity cues that are economically relevant and more directly associated with venture quality, survival, or profitability, such as patent ownership, equity offered, entrepreneurs' education, and financial information. This paper argues that crowdfunding platforms also expose backers to low-validity cues, such as logos and visual design elements, which may have little direct relationship with venture survival but can still influence perception and decision-making. The authors focus on logos because they are salient, widespread, and visually processed by backers. The introduction develops the idea that logo complexity can create processing disfluency, and that this difficulty of processing may be interpreted as uniqueness, originality, novelty, and innovativeness. Since perceived innovativeness can make a venture more attractive, logo complexity may increase funding outcomes even though it is not a direct indicator of venture quality.

sample_or_data: Three studies: one survey examining logo complexity and perceived venture innovativeness, one field study using data from a leading equity crowdfunding platform, and one experiment testing the mechanism underlying the effects of logo complexity.
key_findings: Logo complexity can increase perceived venture innovativeness and positively influence the amount of funds invested in ventures. Backers use the ease or difficulty of processing visual cues as a heuristic when evaluating ventures.

title: Linguistic style and crowdfunding success among social and commercial entrepreneurs
paper_role: empirical fit paper / method paper
context: crowdfunding; entrepreneurial communication; linguistic style; social entrepreneurship; commercial entrepreneurship; online fundraising
main_topic: linguistic style, social categorization, and crowdfunding success
research_question_or_purpose: To examine how the linguistic style of crowdfunding pitches relates to fundraising success and whether this relationship differs between social and commercial entrepreneurs.
abstract: This study examines how the linguistic style of crowdfunding pitches relates to success in raising funds. Drawing on language expectancy theory, the authors argue that the importance of linguistic style depends on whether entrepreneurs belong to an emergent category of new ventures, such as social entrepreneurship, or to a more established category, such as commercial entrepreneurship. Because social entrepreneurs face incomplete social categorization and less clearly formed audience expectations, they rely more on linguistic style to make their campaigns and founders understandable and relatable. Empirical analysis of 656 Kickstarter campaigns shows that linguistic styles that improve understandability and relatability boost the success of social campaigns, but matter much less for commercial campaigns.
introduction: The introduction frames crowdfunding as an increasingly important source of entrepreneurial finance, especially for entrepreneurs who may not have access to traditional funding channels. It emphasizes that crowdfunding campaigns depend heavily on communication because entrepreneurs must persuade a dispersed online crowd through platform-based campaign materials. The paper situates crowdfunding pitches within broader research on entrepreneurial communication, legitimacy, and signaling, arguing that how entrepreneurs communicate may affect whether funders understand, trust, and support them. The introduction also distinguishes social entrepreneurs from commercial entrepreneurs. Social entrepreneurs often operate in an emergent and less clearly categorized venture type, which means audiences may have less stable expectations about what they are, what they offer, and how they should be evaluated. This uncertainty makes linguistic style especially important, because language can help familiarize the crowd with the entrepreneur and the campaign. The study therefore asks whether linguistic style is more consequential for social entrepreneurs than for commercial entrepreneurs in crowdfunding settings.

title: The power of arguments: How entrepreneurs convince stakeholders of the legitimate distinctiveness of their ventures
paper_role: theory foundation / variable-definition paper
context: entrepreneurial rhetoric; stakeholder persuasion; legitimacy; distinctiveness; new venture evaluation
main_topic: how entrepreneurs use arguments to construct legitimate distinctiveness
research_question_or_purpose: To explain how entrepreneurs use different types of arguments to convince stakeholders that their ventures are both legitimate and distinct.
abstract: This article examines how entrepreneurs gain positive stakeholder evaluations by convincing audiences that a new venture is simultaneously legitimate and distinct. Building on prior work on analogies and entrepreneurial narratives, the paper develops a broader typology of rhetorical arguments that entrepreneurs can use to claim legitimacy and support. It also argues that the type of business concept associated with a venture constrains which arguments entrepreneurs can use and how effective those arguments may be. The paper contributes to understanding the micro-discursive processes through which entrepreneurs claim and achieve legitimate distinctiveness.

Stakeholders may hesitate to commit resources unless they can understand why the venture both fits recognizable expectations and stands out from alternatives. Prior research had emphasized analogies and narratives as rhetorical tools, but this paper argues that entrepreneurs use a broader set of arguments to influence stakeholder judgments. The introduction therefore motivates a more systematic typology of arguments that entrepreneurs use to construct legitimacy and distinctiveness.

title: Entrepreneurship, age, and the lifespan: Taking stock and avenues for future research

research_question_or_purpose: To synthesize recent research on age and entrepreneurship and outline future research opportunities for understanding entrepreneurship across the lifespan.
abstract: This editorial argues that entrepreneurship is deeply shaped by age, affecting who enters entrepreneurship, how ventures perform, and whether entrepreneurs persist. Youth may provide resilience and innovation but often comes with limited resources. Midlife may combine skills and experience with tensions around financial security and competing demands. Later life may bring accumulated expertise and networks but also expose entrepreneurs to ageist barriers. The article synthesizes a decade of research and the articles in a special issue, identifying themes and future research directions for understanding entrepreneurship across the lifespan.

Midlife entrepreneurs may have stronger human capital and networks but face opportunity costs, family responsibilities, and financial concerns. Older entrepreneurs may possess expertise and social capital but confront age-based barriers and stereotypes. The article uses this framing to motivate a lifespan perspective that can explain how age-related resources, constraints, motivations, and social expectations shape entrepreneurial action.

abstract: This review examines identity research in entrepreneurship, a central and rapidly growing area of scholarship. The authors systematically review 180 articles from the prior two decades and use bibliometric analysis of keywords, titles, and abstracts to identify co-occurring terms. It then motivates a framework that maps major conversations in identity-in-entrepreneurship research and identifies methodological and theoretical opportunities for future work, including research in digital settings and online communities.

title: The End of Jobs? Paradoxes of Job Deconstruction in Organizations

context: Job deconstruction, task-based work, internal labor markets, adaptive workforces, project-based work structures, and the future of work.

abstract: The paper examines job deconstruction as an emerging organizing paradigm in which traditional jobs are broken down into tasks and projects and then matched with workers' knowledge, skills, and abilities in internal labor markets. title: Lock-In Effects in Online Labor Markets
paper_role: empirical fit paper / theory foundation / method paper / construct-variable paper
context: Online labor markets, reputation mechanisms, platform lock-in, switching costs, reputation portability, platform pricing, worker mobility, and wages.
main_topic: How platform-specific reputation mechanisms create lock-in effects for workers in online labor markets.
research_question_or_purpose: To investigate how platform pricing and platform-specific reputation systems affect workers' switching behavior in online labor markets and whether reputation portability can reduce lock-in effects.
abstract: Online platforms that implement reputation mechanisms typically prevent the transfer of ratings to other platforms, creating lock-in effects and high switching costs for users. This paper theoretically and experimentally investigates the effects of platform pricing on workers' switching behavior in online labor markets and analyzes whether reputation portability can mitigate lock-in effects. The model predicts that platform-specific reputation creates switching costs and allows platforms to capitalize on worker lock-in, while reputation portability lowers switching costs. An online lab-in-the-field experiment supports the theoretical predictions and shows that reputation portability increases worker mobility and wages for highly rated workers.
introduction: The visible article information frames online labor platforms as marketplaces where reputation systems are central to worker success but are usually platform-specific. Because workers cannot easily transfer ratings and reviews across platforms, accumulated reputation becomes a source of switching cost. The article directly connects reputation mechanisms, worker mobility, platform pricing power, fairness perceptions, and wages. This makes it highly relevant for a thesis on digital freelancers, where profile reputation, ratings, and review histories may function as valuable but non-portable marketplace assets.
introduction_key_points: Online labor platforms often use reputation systems that are platform-specific.
Non-portable ratings and reviews create switching costs for workers.
Platform-specific reputation can generate lock-in effects and allow platforms to charge higher fees.
Reputation portability can reduce switching costs and improve worker mobility.
Highly rated workers benefit especially from reputation portability through higher mobility and wages.
method: Theoretical model combined with an online lab-in-the-field experiment.
sample_or_data: Online labor market workers participating in a lab-in-the-field experiment. The visible metadata does not provide the exact sample size.
key_findings: Platform-specific reputation creates switching costs and enables platforms to capitalize on worker lock-in. Reputation portability reduces switching costs, increases worker mobility, and improves wages for highly rated workers. Worker switching is driven primarily by monetary motives, but perceived unfairness of platform fees also matters.
best_use_in_thesis: Use as a core source for the reputation and platform-dependence logic of digital freelancing. It is especially useful for explaining why ratings, reviews, and reputation histories are valuable marketplace assets and why platform-specific reputation can lock freelancers into particular platforms.
notes: Original list item 1. Very strong fit for a freelancer-platform thesis because it directly addresses online labor markets, reputation mechanisms, worker mobility, platform fees, switching costs, and wage outcomes.

abstract: The paper studies two-sided platforms where customers can voice satisfaction through review and rating systems used by platforms to monitor service providers. It argues that customers may misdirect complaints about platform-level features toward individual providers. In a large ride-sharing platform, surge pricing makes drivers more likely to receive complaints, including low ratings or formal complaints. These complaints reduce drivers' future income and offset part of the immediate gain from surged fares. A policy capping surge prices reduces the complaint effect and increases platform usage.

The paper highlights a central problem: customer voice systems may not cleanly separate provider-level quality from platform-level dissatisfaction. Customers may misdirect complaints about platform-level features toward individual providers.
In ride-sharing, surge pricing increases the likelihood of driver complaints.
Complaints negatively affect provider income.
The paper shows that platform design and review systems interact in ways that can distort individual provider reputation.
method: Empirical quantitative analysis of ride-sharing platform data, focusing on the relationship between surge pricing, complaints, ratings, and driver income.

key_findings: Surge pricing increases the likelihood that drivers receive complaints, and these complaints reduce future driver income. title: Freelancing on digital work platforms – roles of virtual community trust and work engagement on person–job fit
journal: VINE Journal of Information and Knowledge Management Systems
paper_role: empirical fit paper / theory foundation / construct-variable paper / method paper
context: Digital work platforms, freelancing, independent contractors, highly specialized knowledge workers, virtual community trust, work engagement, and person-job fit.
main_topic: How virtual community trust and work engagement affect person-job fit among freelancers working on digital work platforms.
research_question_or_purpose: To investigate the impact of virtual community trust on work engagement and person-job fit in the context of digital work platforms.
abstract: The paper investigates the impact of virtual community trust on work engagement and person-job fit among independent contractors working on digital work platforms. Data were collected through an online survey and analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Based on data from 127 experts contracting on digital work platforms, the study finds that virtual community trust positively affects both work engagement and person-job fit, and that work engagement is positively related to person-job fit.
introduction: The visible article information frames the platform economy as a fundamental change in the work environment because it enables alternative work arrangements, temporary organizing, and independent contracting among highly specialized knowledge workers. The paper positions trust among members of virtual platform communities as a key resource for freelancers, because digital work platform participants may lack traditional organizational support structures. The study is directly relevant to digital freelancer research because it connects platform community trust, engagement, and person-job fit in independent platform-based work.

Digital work platforms support temporary organizing and independent contracting among specialized knowledge workers.
Virtual community trust is important for freelancers working through digital platforms.
The study links virtual community trust to work engagement and person-job fit.
The paper provides direct empirical evidence from experts contracting on digital work platforms.
method: Online survey analyzed with confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling.
sample_or_data: 127 experts contracting on digital work platforms.
key_findings: Virtual community trust positively affects both work engagement and person-job fit among experts contracting on digital work platforms. Work engagement also has a significant positive relationship with person-job fit.
